sides.strongest_case: The journal_values option takes back the fix for the one finding the independent review marked critical. §16 found that replay was overstated, and the fix was to carry policy content inline in the journal (§5, lines 149–157, rule T2). The option's own cost line in rulings.jev.json concedes the result: "Replaying a past query's eligibility stays approximate." That breaks principle 2. Caller scopes and context policy change slot outcomes and candidate pools (§3), so a past query replayed against a layer file edited in place gets today's eligibility (§5, line 161). The damage reaches the judge, not just auditing: the one-pass eval-set builder (§6), the byte-identical rebuild (P2), verdict reproduction (P3, V-REPLAY) and V-UNDO all need the composed policy at a past sequence number, and under journal_values that policy is not on any timeline. The "least new machinery" claim is also smaller than it looks. Under journal_values, format 6, `govern` events for the self tier (T4 rollback restores a spec "exactly as an earlier govern event recorded it", §7), constitution events (R5 is settled on seals_and_signing, which signs constitution changes) and `seal` all still have to be built. So one_timeline adds only three things: `reload()` as a journaling op, a `drafts/` folder, and regenerated layers. Validation already exists in v5's shared canonical spec form, with its 60-spec resolver agreement test (§5, lines 154 and 171). For a solo developer on a fixed budget, that is a small addition to a format change he pays for anyway, and it buys one place to audit and one place to seal.
what_must_be_true: The host keeps a full query log: embedding, limit, context, allowed scopes, time and echo (§3, §6, P1/P2). one_timeline alone does not give exact replay; the option's best case is 'from the journal and the host's query log', and SYNAPSE can't log this until mile 3 (§6).

Policy content stays small (§5, line 157): scopes, exclusions, slot selections and a few numbers. If slot selections ever list record ids at scale, carrying them inline bloats the journal and the argument weakens.

v5's `reload()` and both resolvers can be pointed at a spec built from the journal instead of reading layer files directly. This is unverified, because the v5 code isn't on this machine; v5 is assumed to land ([A], mile 0).
Owner context edits really happen during, or between, train and held-out windows. If the owner never edits context layers, the replay gap is only theoretical.
Owner context policy actually changes eligibility at replay. §3 says scopes change slot outcomes [V, v5 code], so the eval set's candidate pools depend on it.
Regenerating derived layers on `reload()` is cheap enough to run on every owner edit. This is unmeasured; fact (d) says it must be measured where it happens.
The R5 seals cover only journal bytes. Under journal_values, owner layer files sit outside tamper evidence unless a second hashing mechanism is added, which amounts to a second timeline.

v1 shows the same failure in miniature, as precedent and not as evidence about v5. `DecayConfig.set_half_life` changes λ in place, with only a log line (src/moneta/decay.py:91-99), and the WAL is deleted at every snapshot (src/moneta/durability.py:119-125). Policy and history that live off a timeline are exactly what v6 exists to stop.
what_would_kill_it: Mile 2 can't test R1 directly: it is Python-only, with no changes to Moneta (§12). Its only route to killing one_timeline is indirect. If v6 itself dies (arm A gains nothing on held-out data, arms D and E both fail, or there is no leverage on SYNAPSE's pool recall at realistic cluster sizes), there's no loop and no referee to keep honest. Exact policy replay then loses its main customer, and journal_values, or no change at all, is the better use of the budget.
Mile 2 finds that eval-set scores barely move when context or scope policy is perturbed. Approximate eligibility would then change no verdict, and the replay gap would cost nothing in practice.
Mile 0 shows that v5's resolvers and `reload()` are tightly coupled to reading layer files, so pointing them at the journal is a large rewrite rather than a small one.
Mile 3 measurements show policy specs are not small (slot selections that grow with record count), or that regenerating derived layers or folding `govern` events at open adds material cost (fact d).
Mile 3's real query logs show that owner context layers never changed inside any train or held-out window over a realistic period.
sides.concession: The reload step is a real workflow cost for this owner in particular. USD and Solaris were chosen partly so policy could be composed and edited live (§5, line 161 names the Solaris edit). Under one_timeline an edit has no effect until `reload()` lints it and journals it, and the derived layers he sees in usdview are read-only in effect (V-DERIVED). For a VFX expert who thinks in live composition, that is a regression. If owner context edits are rare, journal_values keeps the v5 workflow, adds nothing to it, and the approximation may never change a verdict. A reviewer will also point to a middle path: journal a content hash and store a copy in `blobs/<sha>` on each reload. That sounds cheaper. It also needs a reload hook to capture each edit, though. §16 found that naming files by hash alone wasn't enough, because files were edited in place, so hash plus blob is one_timeline with an extra step. Another honest point: under the mile map the extra machinery isn't needed until mile 4. If mile 2 kills v6, deciding R1 now buys nothing. Jev's prior is split. In the as-listed order it leaned journal_values (0.54, confidence about 0.38); reversed, it leaned one_timeline (0.745, confidence about 0.66). It doesn't settle anything either way.
sides.rust_implication: Under one_timeline, the policy at any sequence number is a pure function of the journal bytes. That gives every candidate Rust seam the shape D1 asks for: a pure input (the journal bytes, plus the query log for the eval set) and an exact Python oracle. The verifier and audit (§10) walk a single input, so seal hashes cover record and policy history together. The eval-set builder (§6) is a pure map from journal and query log to a blob, checked byte for byte against its Python version (P2). The WASM referee's input is fixed by that blob. Derived USD layers are an output of the seam, not an input, so Pixar's USD stays outside Rust, as in §10 and §14, and oxideav-usdz stays parked. Under journal_values, any seam that resolves past policy also reads mutable layer files that have no history, so no exact oracle exists for past states, and the audit would need a second, non-journal input. This choice only decides where seams could go. D1 still holds: the scan moves to Rust only if arm P misses the 50 ms p95 gate, and the referee is Rust compiled to WASM because of the sandbox, not for speed.

sides.strongest_case: I'm arguing for journal_values as the next step for v6.0, not as the place v6 should finally end up. one_timeline's events include all of journal_values' events. Both write the loop's tier as `govern{tier: self, why, spec}` with the spec inline (BLUEPRINT_v6 §5, §7 steps 6-7, T4). one_timeline then adds context-tier `govern`, `drafts/`, a journaling `reload()`, derived context layers and journal format 6 (§5 "Format", X2). So moving from journal_values to one_timeline later only adds things and rewrites nothing. Paying for that machinery now means stacking a new journal format on a v5 base that hasn't been merged. Its four lock changes E1-E4 and the half-life call are all still unruled (§1, §14, mile 0 not done). The owner is one developer on a fixed budget, and mile 2 can kill the whole idea (§12). Under the line (§4, L1), everything the loop can change sits in the self tier, and journal_values journals that tier fully. So rollback, V-UNDO, V-HOLD, V-WRITE, C1 and the referee's exactness about the loop's own choices all hold. The approximation is limited to owner context edits, and those are already on the owner's side of the line. It's also bounded. Eval-set features (cosines, deposit order, floors, initial utility, raw attention; §6) don't depend on context policy, so only eligibility (scopes, exclusions, slots) can drift. And because each logged echo carries a fingerprint of the resolved policy (§3 `[V, v5 code]`, §6), the builder can drop any query whose fingerprint no longer matches instead of replaying it wrong. That turns "approximate" into "exact on a filtered subset." With journal_values, mile 3 (query logging and the builder) can start without first owing T2, T3, V-TIMELINE, V-DERIVED and their sabotages, which are mile-4 work.
what_must_be_true: v5 lands with its resolved-policy fingerprint in the echo intact (§3 [V, v5 code]), so the builder can detect queries whose context policy has since changed and drop them, instead of replaying them under today's scopes.

Owner context edits are rare compared with the train and held-out windows (§6). If they are rare, dropping fingerprint-mismatched queries costs little eval-set coverage and doesn't skew the sample toward quiet contexts.

Moving from journal_values to one_timeline later really only adds things: self-tier `govern` events written under journal_values keep the same `{tier, name, why, spec}` shape, so a later format bump can add context-tier events without rewriting history (§5).

The self layer can still be placed as the weakest sublayer (C1) and resolved from journaled values while the owner's layers stay files edited in place. In other words, the C3 resolver-agreement test extends to a stack where only the self layer is derived.
In v6.0 the referee scores only self-tier candidates (§4 'Self' tier, L2), so the referee and V-REPLAY need exact history only for the self tier, plus fingerprint-filtered queries.
Mile 2 is still a Python-only experiment with no changes to Moneta (§12), so nothing in milestones 2-3 depends on a format-6 journal.
what_would_kill_it: Mile 2, arm E (owner sample, about 200 queries): if recovering half of arm A's held-out gain breaks down under small label perturbations or a small loss of queries, then eligibility drift from even one mid-window owner edit can flip a verdict, and filtering by fingerprint isn't safe. That argues for one_timeline.

Mile 2, arm D under systematic bias: if the loop's margin (J4, the session bootstrap) only fires reliably on a complete, unfiltered eval set, then dropping fingerprint-mismatched queries removes the statistical power the margin needs.
Mile 2 pool-host sweep: if leverage on pool recall is concentrated in particular contexts or slot outcomes, eligibility becomes the main channel of the effect and can't be treated as noise.

Mile 3 evidence that the owner edits context layers often (for example, Solaris edits most sessions). Then the fingerprint filter discards most of the log and the replay gap from §16 is in effect permanent.

v5's merge drops or changes the policy fingerprint in the echo, or it turns out not to cover scopes and slot selections. That removes the mitigation, and journal_values goes back to plain approximation.
The second-opinion review of §15 Q1 finds a read input that only a journaled context policy can pin down. If so, the fingerprint filter can't make even a subset exact.
sides.concession: one_timeline is the better design to end up with. journal_values leaves the critical finding from the independent review unresolved: §16 "Replay was overstated" names exactly this gap, and one_timeline is the fix §5 was written to apply ("This closes a gap v5 leaves open"). Under journal_values, principle 2 ("every answer and every verdict can be re-derived") holds for the loop's tier and for fingerprint-filtered queries, but not for owner edits in general. Principle 1 ("nothing is ever edited") is openly broken for owner layers, which stay edited in place. V-TIMELINE and V-DERIVED can't be written as specified. The Solaris drift risk that §16 flagged also comes back, because a live-view edit lands directly in a file that recall reads. On the Jev evidence, the more confident answer went the other way, and my side can't claim it. In the reversed order (layer_chain, journal_values, one_timeline, none), one_timeline won from third position at a mean of 0.745, with confidence 0.65-0.67 on both repeats. journal_values' win in the listed order was weaker (0.54, confidence 0.36-0.41). That doesn't look like a first-position artifact. It's a firmer lean toward one_timeline than toward my option. Last, if the owner expects to need exact owner-edit history anyway by mile 4, deferring it costs a later format migration, and that migration has to happen on a journal that already holds real data.
sides.rust_implication: Under D1 (Rust only behind a pure seam with an exact oracle; §10), R1 doesn't change the referee seam. The WASM referee reads one flat buffer of pool features, labels and candidate values under either option, and the mile-2 Python referee stays its oracle (V-POOL, V-EXP). R1 does affect the verifier and audit seam. Under journal_values, a Rust seal and audit walker targets the journal format v5 already has plus the self-tier `govern` and `seal` events. That's a small, stable byte format whose Python oracle can be fixed early, which is what D1's exact oracle needs. Under one_timeline, the verifier targets format 6, which keeps changing until mile 4 (context-tier `govern`, journaling reload, derived-layer regeneration), so the oracle would have to be rewritten as that format settles. The eval-set builder stays a pure, deterministic function of (journal, query log) under either option, so it's still eligible for a Rust port later. Under journal_values, though, its inputs don't include historical owner policy, so its oracle is exact only on the fingerprint-filtered subset. The scan decision is unchanged either way: arm P first, and Rust only if it misses the 50 ms p95 gate (v5's 161 ms at 10k records is about 3x over; §10, §11). For reference, v1's tunable already has a bounded, config-level setter (src/moneta/decay.py:91-99 enforces [MIN, MAX]; src/moneta/api.py:129 `half_life_seconds`), and its clamp on negative time steps (src/moneta/decay.py:63-65) is the monotonicity premise V-POOL relies on. v1 isn't the base for v6, though: its query writes state through decay_all (src/moneta/api.py:401), which is why purity comes from v5 and not from v1.

sides.strongest_case:
Jev gives no prior here. As listed it leaned to recall_half_life (0.61 vs 0.38). Reversed it was a coin flip (0.49 vs 0.495, and that run did not repeat stably; summary.json r2_first_knob). So the case has to rest on the design itself.

1. **The experiment is already built for this knob.** Mile 2 is the cheap go/no-go. Its known answer is a sweep of the recall half-life, its world has a hidden fade rate, and its kill rule already names β as the fallback: "try R2's other knob" (BLUEPRINT_v6 §12; summary at line 27). If β goes first, a solo developer has to redesign the experiment's ground truth before running the one cheap test. Under recall_half_life, β stays the free second shot.

2. **The half-life is the knob that matches the question.** The question is how fast usefulness fades in ranking. β can't reorder records the same way. It is a monotone transform of a fixed U, so records with equal cosine keep their order. It also can't change how old attention weighs against recent attention, and that weighting is where the echo pathology lives (§3).

3. **v1 already treats the half-life as the knob.** It has bounds of 60 s to 24 h (src/moneta/decay.py:30-35). It can be changed at runtime (decay.py:91-105). It is "explicitly provisional" until "load testing produces curves" (decay.py:18-21). The loop is the curve-producer v1 asked for, and the constitution's bounds already exist.

4. **The split keeps the tiers separate.** Under β, ranking still reads retention utility. Every owner amendment to the retention half-life would then silently move the tuned β's optimum, which breaks the separation between the constitution tier and the self tier (§4 tier table). The split removes that coupling.
what_must_be_true: Owner rules v5's 'half-life reinterprets history' call in favor (BLUEPRINT_v6 §14 row 'The half-life reinterprets history'): the §4 split and the derived recall fold rest on it.

E2 (reads never write) lands with v5. In v1 the split is impossible because query() mutates utility in place via ecs.decay_all (src/moneta/api.py:401; ecs.py:222), so ranking utility and retention utility are the same stored number.
Ranking signal really varies with fade rate. In the §12 world, the half-life sweep under arm A shows a non-flat held-out curve on at least one host at realistic cluster sizes.

The recall-anchor rebuild on a repoint (one pass over attention events, §4; §11 table row 'Rebuilding recall anchors on a repoint' [U]) is cheap enough at 10k-100k records that probation/repoint stays practical.
The §6 exact-pool monotonicity argument holds for the second λ through floor and clamp (V-POOL), relying on the negative-Δt clamp at decay.py:61-67.
Every compat surface (Memory.utility, v1 snapshot.json, USD projection) keeps reporting retention utility, and explain() shows both (§4), so SYNAPSE sees no change.
what_would_kill_it: The §12 kill rule fires: under arm A (oracle), the recall-half-life line search gains nothing on the held-out window (days 91-120) on either host.

In mile 2, a β sweep (cheap to add as a diagnostic, since the ranking math is re-implemented in Python anyway) recovers about the same arm-A held-out gain as the half-life sweep. Then the half-life's extra expressiveness is not used, and the split's cost buys nothing. This is likely if attention is sparse: for never-attended records, U^β ≈ U0^β·e^(-βλΔt), so β acts as a rescaled λ.

No leverage: the half-life cannot move SYNAPSE-shaped pool recall at realistic cluster sizes, while β can (β also reweights the floor, floor^β, which may matter more for which records enter a 50-candidate pool).
Measured recall-anchor rebuild or seal cost (§5 seal, line ~175) is large enough to make repoint/rollback slow, which undercuts the line's 'pointer-reversible' promise in practice.
The owner rules v5's history-reinterpretation call against it, or rejects the split. The blueprint then already names β as the fallback (§4 last paragraph).
sides.concession:
β is much cheaper, and on a fixed solo budget that matters.

**What the split costs.** It adds a second derived fold per record, recall anchors in every seal (§5), and a dual-utility explain() and recall_utility surface (§4). It adds a rebuild cost that hasn't been measured, and it depends on a v5 call the owner hasn't ruled on (§14).

**What β costs.** It needs none of that. Its exact-pool argument is trivial: U ∈ [floor, 1], so U^β is monotone in β. In v1 terms it is a one-token change at src/moneta/api.py:414 (`max(cos_sim, 0.0) * memory.utility`), and it reproduces v5 exactly at β = 1. For unattended records, β also approximates a half-life change.

**Bottom line.** If mile 2 shows β gets most of the gain, β should win on cost. The honest position is: half-life first because the experiment and v1 are built around it, with β swept alongside in mile 2 as a near-free diagnostic.
sides.rust_implication:
**This option adds no new transcendental function.**

The recall half-life reuses the decay formula verbatim (§14 lock), with a second λ. The only libm function that has to match exactly is still exp, which V-EXP already covers (§6).

β would add pow(U, β) to the scoring path. That is a second function that isn't correctly rounded, and it would need its own Python/WASM agreement check. For non-integer β near the floor, last-bit differences can flip near-ties.

**Where the Rust seam goes, under D1.** Rust comes in only if arm P misses its latency gate. The natural seam is the recall fold: a pure batch function from (attention events, λ_recall, floor, clamp) to recall anchors.
- **The oracle** is v1/v5's Python decay_value (src/moneta/decay.py:48-69), including the negative-Δt clamp.
- **The checks** are the existing V-EXP and V-POOL. V-POOL already has the clamp-removal sabotage.
- **One exp implementation** should be shared between the read path and the WASM referee, so exactness never relies on the 'ties within one ulp' fallback.

This seam is also the likeliest place to miss the gate, because a repoint rebuilds every record's recall anchors in one pass (§4, cost [U]). So it is both the most useful place to measure and the cleanest seam to put behind an exact oracle.

The referee needs no anchors, since its features are raw attention history (§6). The same pure fold kernel can therefore serve both the read path and the referee.

sides.strongest_case: The exponent is the only R2 option that the loop can tune without first settling a ruling that hasn't been made. The blueprint says plainly that the half-life split "rests on" v5's unruled call that the half-life reinterprets history (§14 lock table, §4). Mile 0 isn't done either (§12). By contrast, score = max(cos,0) × U^β with β = 1 reproduces v1/v5 ranking exactly (src/moneta/api.py:414; src/moneta/ecs.py:294). It leaves every v1 retention surface alone: no second fold, no rebuild of recall anchors on a repoint (cost marked [U] in §4 and §11), no recall anchors inside seals (§5), no `recall_utility` field, no two-utility `explain()`, and no compatibility exposure for SYNAPSE's `Memory.utility` or `snapshot.json`. Reviewer question §15.5 doesn't come up at all. For a solo developer on a fixed budget, that is a whole subsystem not built and not tested. It also serves principle 2 and the exact-pool claim better. U^β is monotone non-increasing in β for U in [floor, 1], so V-POOL's corner argument becomes a short proof, not an argument through the attention fold, its floors and its clamps (§6). The referee only needs one fixed retention-utility feature per candidate, not a replay of raw attention history, so eval sets are smaller and the referee's fuel use is easier to bound. Finally, the exponent is the most direct lever on what §3 identifies as the threat. SYNAPSE's echo attention inflates U for whatever already ranked well, and β < 1 (down to β → 0, which is pure cosine) is exactly "trust utility less". That gives the loop a falsifiable, already-known baseline.
what_must_be_true: The main way ranking goes wrong is how much utility should weigh against similarity, not the decay timescale. Echo-inflated U (§3) is the candidate cause, and it hasn't been shown to dominate [U].
The best β is measurably different from 1 on held-out data. If it isn't, the exponent has no leverage, which is the same 'knob is wrong' risk §12 names for the half-life.

A correctly implemented pow(U, 1.0) returns U exactly, so the β=1 oracle matches v1 bit-for-bit. Equivalently, the read path special-cases β=1. V-EXP becomes V-POW and must still count ulp disagreements at β≠1.
Bounds on β stay strictly above 0 (or 0^0 is defined explicitly), so U = floor = 0 never produces an undefined score.

Retention utility at query time is a legitimate fixed eval-set feature. It depends only on the owner's retention half-life, which lives in the constitution (§4 tier table), so a change to that half-life is an amendment that rebuilds the eval set. That is acceptable.
The owner values not depending on the unruled v5 half-life call, and not building the recall-utility split, more than the extra expressiveness of tuning fade.
what_would_kill_it: In mile 2, arm A on the direct host finds a held-out gain for the recall half-life, but the best β ≈ 1 or β gives no significant gain. That shows the decay timescale is the error and the exponent can't reach it.

On the SYNAPSE-shaped pool host, at realistic cluster sizes, sweeping β moves pool recall clearly less than sweeping the half-life does. Leverage on the first host is what matters (§12 kill criterion 3).

The world's failure turns out to be one of order among utilities, for example stale but heavily attended records outranking fresh ones at similar cosine. U^β is a monotone transform of U, so it can never reorder two records with equal cosine and can't fix this.
Arms D or E recover half of arm A's gain with the half-life but not with β. That would mean the exponent is the weaker signal for noisy labels.
V-POW finds pow disagreements between the Python and WASM/libm builds that flip near-ties more often than the attention fold's exp disagreements do.
The owner rules the v5 half-life call anyway, and accepts the split, at mile 0. That removes the exponent's main sequencing advantage.
sides.concession: The exponent can't change how memory fades, and fading is what the blueprint's own world simulates. The mile-2 world gives each record's true usefulness a hidden half-life (§12). The known-answer sweep, the line search, the `recallHalfLife` policy field (§5) and the worked proposal (§7) are all built around the half-life. The exponent is a monotone transform of U, so it preserves the order of utilities among records. If v5's single half-life is simply wrong for ranking, β can only re-weight a mis-ordered signal, never correct it. The half-life is also easier to explain to an owner ("ranking forgets in 14 days") than "utility raised to 0.6". The honest middle path costs little: run the β sweep as a parallel arm in mile 2, since it's minutes of Python. If the half-life wins there by a clear held-out margin, the exponent's simplicity advantage doesn't justify picking the knob that can't reach the error.
sides.rust_implication: Under D1, Rust enters only behind a pure seam with an exact oracle, and only if arm P misses its latency gate. The exponent makes that seam as small as it can be. The referee or scan kernel becomes a stateless map over a flat buffer of (cos, U, label) tuples, computing max(cos,0) × pow(U, β) and then top-k. The oracle is trivial: at β=1 it must match v1's Python product (src/moneta/api.py:414) bit-for-bit. At β≠1 there is one transcendental per candidate, checked by a V-POW count against the Python reference. The recall half-life would instead push a stateful fold across the seam: per-event exp decay with a floor, the negative-Δt clamp (src/moneta/decay.py:66-69) and a clamp to 1 (src/moneta/ecs.py:211-212), over each candidate's raw attention history. That means a larger buffer, unmeasured fuel and memory needs (§6, §11), and ulp error that compounds per event, which V-EXP flags as an open threat (§6). So the exponent keeps the Rust/WASM seam at "score a flat pool". The attention fold and the retention fold stay in Python (v5's existing code) with no second Rust implementation to keep in sync. That keeps the Rust surface small enough that a solo developer can maintain both sides and the oracle.

sides.strongest_case: For v6.0, owner labels are the only source that can both move the first host's metric and end the chain of judges where principle 4 requires. Use signals cannot move pool recall at all (BLUEPRINT §6, "Shown-only labels can't improve a pool host"; §12 arm C "can't win by construction"). That means mixed's whole signal pipeline adds nothing for SYNAPSE: all of mixed's leverage on pool recall comes from its model-label half, so it costs two pipelines (§6 table) and buys one. Model labels and owner labels both cover unshown records, but only the owner's labels carry the owner's own meaning of "better recall." The core is creative-agnostic and "the host and the owner define what better recall means" (facts; §6 "The objective belongs to the owner"; J2). Model labels quietly bring in a third party's idea of relevance, the same worry §15 Q8 raises about shipping nDCG@k as a default. They also have a verification gap. A model's systematic bias, which is the failure arm D exists to probe (§12, §15 "How much systematic label bias the loop tolerates is unknown"), can only be measured against a trusted reference. On a real store that reference is a set of owner labels. So owner labels have to come first under either path. Model labels can be added later by amendment once they are calibrated against that set. Finally, R5 has settled on owner ed25519 signatures (summary.json, r5 settled at 0.895/0.925). If the owner signs thousands of model labels he never read, the signature stops meaning "I judged this" and becomes a rubber stamp, which weakens the attribution R5 is meant to provide.
what_must_be_true: A sample of about 200 queries labeled on the full candidate pool is enough to recover a meaningful share of the oracle's held-out gain on at least one host. This is §12 arm E's pass condition: arm D or E reaching at least half of arm A's held-out gain.

Each query's labeling job is bounded. The owner labels the exact candidate pool reachable under the tunable's bounds (the §6 corner argument, checked by V-POOL), which is roughly 50 to a few hundred records per query. That is not the whole store. The real store is small: §12 mile 0 cites 841 records.

With about 200 queries grouped into sessions, the session-resampled paired bootstrap (J4, §6) can still yield a margin that a real gain clears. Correlated sessions do not shrink the effective sample until nothing can promote.
The held-out window (§6, 'The holdout is the future') wears out slowly enough that the owner can relabel a fresh window between amendments at a sustainable rate.
The owner's judgments are consistent enough over time to act as ground truth. Arm E models them as noise-free true relevance, and the real owner is not noise-free.
One knob (R2) and a loop held behind owner_gate (R4, settled at 0.945/0.875) do not need the large continuous label volume that only a model can supply.
what_would_kill_it: Mile 2 reports that arm E fails to recover at least half of arm A's held-out gain on either host while arm D does, including under the systematic-bias noise model. That would show the small owner sample is the bottleneck, not label quality. §12's rescope clause ('larger owner-labeled sets') would then need a volume the owner's budget cannot supply.

Mile 2 shows that arm E's training signal is too thin for the session-level bootstrap margin (J4) to clear, so the loop never promotes even where arm A does. V-MARGIN would pass trivially because nothing moves.

Arm D under systematic bias (recency or high cosine) still lands within the search resolution of arm A's swept optimum. That would weaken the claim that model bias is the dominant risk and make model labels' coverage worth their cost.

The measured pool size per query at realistic cluster sizes (§12 sweeps cluster size against the 50-candidate pool) makes owner labeling of each pool impractical, for example thousands of judgments per refresh of the held-out window.

Arm A itself cannot move SYNAPSE's pool recall at realistic cluster sizes (§12 'No leverage on SYNAPSE'). Every label ruling would then be moot for the first host. It would not refute owner_labels specifically, but it would remove its main advantage over use signals.
sides.concession: The weakest part of this case is volume and freshness, and mile 2 is set up in a way that may flatter it. Arm E gives the owner perfect true relevance on 200 queries. A real owner gets tired, drifts, and labels the same record differently a month later. Owner labeling also cannot easily rule on records it never sees: deciding that an unshown record is relevant means reviewing the whole reachable pool, roughly 50 or more records per query, so 200 queries is about 10,000 judgments per labeled window. That has to be redone as the held-out window wears out (§15). For a solo developer on a fixed budget, the owner's attention is the scarcest resource in the project. Model labels at a pinned version with recorded request hashes (P4; the Jev verdict cache is [V, offline]) cost little money at an 841-record scale. They are fully replayable, and they keep pace as the store grows. If arm D with systematic bias still clears the pass bar, mixed (or plain model labels calibrated against a small owner audit set) is the better engineering choice, and owner_labels turns into the calibration set rather than the label source. On honest terms, model_labels' "costs money per label" point is weak at this scale. The real argument against it is unmeasured bias and diluted signatures, not price.
sides.rust_implication: Under D1 (Rust only behind a pure seam with an exact oracle, §10), choosing owner labels adds no Rust seam and narrows the existing one. Labels are data in the referee's single flat buffer (§6, "reads one flat buffer of pool features, labels and candidate values"), so the source of the labels never touches the read path or the scan. The scan decision stays as D1 has it: arm P first, Rust only if the 50 ms p95 gate is missed. Owner labeling is a human workflow, and model labeling is network I/O, so neither is a pure compute seam with an oracle, and neither has a case for Rust. A small owner-labeled eval set does three things. (1) It keeps the WASM referee (the one Rust-to-WASM seam marked [P] in §10) well inside the toy's caps of 20M fuel and 8 MB, so the open question 'Mile 2 measures what a realistic eval set needs' resolves cheaply. (2) It makes the Python referee from mile 2 a fast, exact oracle for V-POOL and V-EXP. (3) It has one real downside: fewer pooled records means fewer near-ties for V-EXP to find, so the exp() disagreement between Rust/libm and the platform's exp is sampled more thinly. A larger, synthetic or model-labeled pool may be needed only for that conformance test. That is separate from the label source the loop is judged by. The settled R5 seal walk and audit (§10 'The verifier') stay the second Rust candidate, unaffected by R3. No Rust code is justified by this ruling, and the v1 decay clamp at src/moneta/decay.py:65-67, which the V-POOL monotonicity argument depends on, is unaffected.

sides.option: mixed (use signals on shown records + pinned model labels on unshown candidates, signed together)
sides.strongest_case: The blueprint's own design creates a recurring demand for labels that owner_labels can't meet. The holdout is a time split that wears out, and an amendment rolls both dates forward (§6 l.213-216, §15 l.493). Each roll-forward needs fresh labels on fresh queries, and the rulings file itself lists owner_labels' cost as "small, slow to refresh". Mixed produces labels mechanically and is bounded by the window by construction. A labeler fed only the journal prefix can't see the future, while an owner labeling a months-old query has the hindsight that "a label may only use events inside its own query's window" forbids (§6 l.217, V-HOLDOUT l.343). It also spends the owner's scarcest resource best, given the solo-developer fixed-budget fact. Under mixed the owner signs a recorded batch (P4 l.209, R5 settled on seals_and_signing) rather than producing each label by hand. The Jev verdict cache already records the version pin plus the request hash `[V, offline]` (l.44, l.209). Finally, mixed is the only option with an internal audit: on shown records the two sources overlap, so their disagreement rate is a direct, continuous estimate of the model bias that fact (a) warns about (l.82). Neither single source can give that, and it keeps "nothing judges itself" (principle 4) honest for the model half.
what_must_be_true: Arm D (model labels on the full pool, l.405) recovers at least half of arm A's held-out gain under the SYSTEMATIC bias model (recency/high-cosine), not only random flips, on at least one host (pass rule l.410). Mile 2 has no mixed arm, so mixed's unshown half stands or falls through D.
Arm E (~200 owner-labeled queries, l.406) is insufficient or too costly to refresh. If 200 queries suffice and the owner can re-label them at each holdout roll-forward, mixed has no case on cost.

Model-label spend per refresh fits the fixed budget. The pool is max(3 x limit, 50) per query (§3 l.99), so a refresh means 50+ judgments per logged query. Per-label cost is [U]; no figure is assumed here.

SYNAPSE agrees to change what its attention means from 'ranked well' (top five reranked, §3 l.97) to 'was used'. That is SYNAPSE's call (§15 l.495). v1's signal_attention takes Dict[UUID, float] with no retrieved-vs-used distinction (src/moneta/api.py:420-433), so the use half is a host change, not a Moneta change.

Use-signal and model-label disagreement on shown records is informative about model error on unshown records, i.e. bias on the shown set roughly transfers. If shown and unshown records differ systematically (fact c), the audit underestimates the bias.
The label builder can be restricted to the journal prefix plus the query log (P1/P2), so model labels satisfy V-HOLDOUT mechanically.

Mixed labels carry per-label provenance (source, weight, pin, request hash) so the referee and tripwires can weight or exclude a source. Otherwise the two pipelines collapse into one unauditable label stream.
what_would_kill_it: Arm D fails to recover half of arm A's held-out gain under the systematic-bias noise model on BOTH hosts (l.405, l.410). That kills the unshown half, and with it mixed's only advantage on the pool host.

Arm E recovers at least half of arm A's gain at ~200 queries on the pool host (l.406). Owner labels are then enough, cheaper to build (one pipeline, no host change, no model spend), and more trusted: owner_labels wins.
Arm A can't move pool recall at realistic cluster sizes (kill rule l.416). No label source matters for SYNAPSE then, and mixed's two-pipeline cost buys nothing.
Mile 3 shows SYNAPSE can't or won't emit true use signals, or that doing so distorts utility in ways the owner rejects (§15 l.495). Mixed then degrades to model_labels and should be ruled as that.
Use-signal vs model-label agreement on shown records turns out uninformative about unshown-record error, i.e. the audit doesn't transfer. That removes the calibration argument.
sides.concession: owner_labels has real strengths. It is the most trusted source by the rulings file's own wording. It covers unshown records, which is the one property the pool host needs (§6 l.207). It needs no SYNAPSE change, no model spend and only one pipeline, and arm E tests it directly while nothing in mile 2 tests mixed. Jev leaned owner_labels in both orders (0.555 as listed, 0.54 reversed), while mixed collapsed from 0.17 to 0.045 when the order flipped, so mixed's prior is position-fragile. The sharpest point: on the SYNAPSE-shaped host, the use-signal half contributes nothing to pool recall by construction. Anything shown was already in the incumbent's pool (§6 l.207), so there mixed is model_labels plus a second pipeline whose only job is calibration, and that pipeline requires a host change. For a solo developer on a fixed budget, two pipelines is a real cost, not a footnote. An honest version of mixed probably still wants a small owner audit set to anchor the model-bias estimate, which narrows the gap between the options. The fair synthesis is to rule owner_labels for mile 3 if arm E passes, and to rule mixed only if E is too small or too slow to refresh and D survives systematic bias.
sides.rust_implication: Under D1, labeling creates no Rust seam. There is no model in the read path (§14 l.477), and labeling is I/O-bound on model calls, so it stays in Python. The seam mixed touches is the referee's input ABI. The WASM referee reads one flat buffer of pool features, labels and candidate values (§6 l.239). Mixed requires that buffer to carry per-label provenance (source tag use/model, weight, and a pin/request-hash reference), so the referee can weight sources and tripwires can report per-source disagreement. That makes the buffer schema part of the pinned contract, with the mile 2 Python referee as its exact oracle (§10 l.351; V-POOL/V-EXP). The eval-set builder's label merge is a pure, byte-identical function of journal + query log + label cache (P2). It is a Rust candidate only if mile 3 measures it slow, with the Python version as the oracle. The V-HOLDOUT label-window check is also a pure function of bytes and could sit in the Rust verifier beside the seal walk (§10 l.352). owner_labels puts none of this pressure on the seam: its label set is tiny and single-source, so the referee buffer stays simpler.

r4.attack:
owner_gate is still the right direction, but the settlement does not hold as stated. Under the blueprint's own facts it is under-specified in four places, and the order check that 'settled' it never tested owner_gate's position.

(1) THE ROLLBACK LEAK. This breaks the line under every R4 option, and owner_gate does not close it. §4 holds sleep passes during probation (J7), but 'Attention from probation stays in the journal' and only the eval-set builder filters it by generation. The retention fold still counts it. Take a SYNAPSE-shaped host: it signals attention on its own top 5 (§3), so under generation N+1 it attends to a different set of records. The owner then rolls back, which is not adoption, so the effects do not fall on the owner's side under §4's own reasoning. The hold lifts, and the next sleep pass tombstones by a utility and attention count that the rolled-back generation shaped. In v1 the prune key is `memory.utility < PRUNE_UTILITY_THRESHOLD and memory.attended_count < PRUNE_ATTENDED_THRESHOLD` (src/moneta/consolidation.py:110-114), fed by reduce_attention_log (src/moneta/attention_log.py:108-135), so attended_count moves with attention whatever the decay. Records that N+1 kept surfacing are protected, and records it pushed out lose their bumps, after a rollback the owner meant as 'undo'. V-UNDO only probes answers at a pinned seq. It never runs a post-rollback sleep pass, so its sabotage misses this. Agent deposits made during probation, written from different recall, are journal events too and survive the rollback.

(2) APPROVAL IS UNAUTHENTICATED UNLESS R4 IS COUPLED TO R5. 'The substrate files a request and the owner approves': the approval reaches the substrate as an input on the loop machine. L3 only says the substrate writes the journal. R5's signed set covers 'constitution changes and seals', not promote, adopt or rollback govern events (§5, §7). A buggy or compromised process can append govern{why: adopt}. That ends probation and releases irreversible retention, so the substrate approves itself, against principle 4. owner_gate only means something if each promote and adopt carries an owner signature verified against a pinned key.

(3) NO TIMEOUT, NO DEFAULT. The facts say a solo owner on a fixed budget. §4 and §15 admit 'memory grows without retention' and 'how long probation can safely last is unknown'. owner_gate also takes two owner acts per change: approve the promotion, then adopt it (§7 steps 5-7). Approval followed by owner absence holds retention indefinitely. Any timeout rule, such as auto-rollback, is a pointer move without a human. That contradicts J6 unless it is carved out explicitly. Also unspecified: a second promotion request while generation N is still unadopted, and which spec a rollback restores in that case.

(4) THE HELD-OUT WINDOW LEAKS THROUGH THE OWNER. §7 step 5 puts tripwires, including the held-out window, into the evidence the owner sees. J3 hides held-out scores from the loop, but an owner who approves or rejects on them, cycle after cycle, is selecting on the holdout (fact b). That wears out the window faster than §6 plans for, and nothing marks it as worn out.

(5) TIMING. Miles 3-4 run in shadow (§12), and V-SHADOW tests a mode where the pointer never moves. owner_gate only describes mile 5. Ruling it now is fine as the end state, but the operative state until mile 5 is shadow_only.
r4.residual_risk: If ruled as-is: tombstones after a rollback that were shaped by the rolled-back generation, which is irreversible (v5's fold has no path back from a tombstone, §4); forged adopt events releasing held retention; retention held without bound when the owner is unavailable; and a held-out window worn out by owner selection. Minimum patch before the ruling stands: (a) on rollback, the retention fold excludes, or the next sleep pass refuses to act on, attention tagged with the rolled-back generation, and V-UNDO gains a sabotage that runs a sleep pass after rollback; (b) promote, adopt and rollback are owner-signed and fall under R5's signed set; (c) a constitution-set probation ceiling with an explicit default action, either auto-rollback carved out of J6 or retention stays held with an alarm, plus a rule of one pending generation at a time; (d) owner-facing evidence shows held-out pass/fail only, or each disclosure is counted against the window's wear.

r5.attack:
seals_and_signing beats the alternatives, but as specified it cannot meet the blueprint's own check, and it leaves the most dangerous acts unsigned.

(1) V-SEAL'S TAIL CLAUSE IS UNACHIEVABLE WITH SEALS ALONE. §9 V-SEAL requires that 'an edit after the last seal fails at open'. A seal records a running hash only up to its own sequence number (§5, T5). Lines after the last seal carry only v5's CRC-32, which §5 itself says anyone can recompute. So a deliberate edit to the unsealed tail passes at open. Meeting V-SEAL needs a per-line running hash, or an equivalent hash carried in each event, at least from the v6 genesis on. Separately, the cost given against per_line_chain ('changes every v5 journal line') is mostly moot. §5 Format already has a v6 journal declare format 6 and a v5 reader refuse it, so v6 already breaks line compatibility. The chain can start at the v6 genesis without rewriting v5 history.

(2) THE SIGNING GAP. The key is off the loop machine, but the substrate writes seals periodically on the loop machine. So seals are unsigned when written, and the owner signs them later in batches. Every seal after the last owner-signed one has exactly seals_only's weakness: a full rewrite with recomputed hashes passes. For a solo owner on a budget, that window could be weeks.

(3) TRUNCATION AND ROLLBACK ATTACKS. If signed seals live inside the journal, cutting off the journal before the latest signed seal leaves a shorter, fully valid history. Running hashes and signatures cannot detect missing suffixes. That needs an external anchor: the owner keeps the latest signed seal's seq and hash off-machine, and the verifier demands a journal at least that long.

(4) TRUST ROOT NOT PINNED. Verification needs the owner's public key. If it sits in the trust store on the loop machine, the same one that pins the referee hash (J1), an attacker can swap in their own key and re-sign everything. The key has to be pinned out of band, in the code-ceiling tier (X1) or a signed genesis. The J1 trust store must itself be signed, or the referee pin goes around the constitution's signature.

(5) THE SIGNED SET IS TOO NARROW. Only 'constitution changes and seals' are signed. Not signed: govern adopt, promote and rollback, which release irreversible retention (see R4); reload() context edits (T3), which change scopes and slot winners and so change answers; and owner_gate approvals. Attribution fails for exactly the acts whose effects cannot be undone.

(6) KEY LIFECYCLE. 'Cost: key handling' hides rotation and loss. A lost key freezes the constitution for good. Rotation must be an event signed by the old key, and recovery needs a pre-registered second key. None of this is specified, and the owner works on Windows, which §15 says is untested.
r5.residual_risk: If ruled as-is: undetected edits to the unsealed tail, which also fails V-SEAL; forgeable history back to the last owner-signed seal; silent truncation; key substitution through an unpinned trust store; and unattributable adopt and reload events that drive irreversible retention. Minimum patch: a per-event running hash from the v6 genesis (a hybrid of seals and per_line_chain, with no v5 rewrite), a signed set extended to every govern event with why in {adopt, promote, rollback, amend} plus T3 reloads and the trust store, an external anchor of the latest signed seal, the public key pinned in code or genesis, and a rotation and recovery protocol. Without these, the ruling should read 'seals_and_signing, amended'.
